title: Exploring Some Geometric Themes
subject: Maths-2
description: Fractals (Sierpinski Carpet and Triangle, Koch Snowflake) and visualising solids: profiles, faces/edges/vertices, nets, shortest paths on a cuboid, projections and views, shadows, and isometric drawing.

questions.question: Which property makes a shape a fractal?
options: the same or a similar pattern repeats at smaller and smaller scales
it has exactly four lines of symmetry and four equal sides
it is made only of straight edges that meet at right angles
it tiles the whole plane without leaving any gaps or overlaps
questions.explanation: The chapter defines fractals as self-similar shapes: they show the same or a similar pattern over and over again at smaller and smaller scales. Symmetry, straight edges and tiling are different geometric ideas.

questions.question: Why is a fern described as a natural fractal?
options: its leaves are all exactly the same size and shape as each other
its leaves are smaller copies of the fern, and so are their sub-leaves
its stem is perfectly straight and divides into exactly two branches
its leaves grow only on one side of the stem in a straight row
questions.explanation: The fern has smaller copies of itself as its leaves, and these in turn have even smaller copies as sub-leaves, and so on — that repeated self-similarity is what makes it a fractal.

questions.question: Select ALL the natural objects the chapter lists as showing self-similarity.
options: coastlines
lightning
rainbows
soap bubbles
questions.explanation: The chapter names trees, clouds, coastlines, mountains and lightning as natural examples of self-similarity. Rainbows and soap bubbles are not in the list — a rainbow's bands do not contain smaller rainbows.

questions.question: Sierpinski, who discovered the Sierpinski Carpet and Gasket, was a mathematician from which country?
options: Sweden
Holland
Greece
Poland
questions.explanation: The chapter calls Sierpinski 'the Polish mathematician'. Von Koch (Snowflake) was Swedish, Escher (fractal art) was Dutch; Greece is only mentioned for the word 'isometric'.

questions.question: Who first described the Koch Snowflake, and when?
options: Von Koch, a Swedish mathematician, in 1904
Von Koch, a Polish mathematician, in 1904
Sierpinski, a Polish mathematician, in 1904
Escher, a Dutch artist, in the year 1904
questions.explanation: The Koch Snowflake is named after the Swedish mathematician Von Koch, who first described it in 1904. Sierpinski (Polish) is linked to the Carpet and Gasket, and Escher was a Dutch artist, not a mathematician.

questions.question: The Kandariya Mahadev Temple is described as fractal-like because
options: its walls are tiled with identical squares of a single size
the tower carries smaller copies of itself, then smaller still
its plan is a perfect pyramid with four triangular faces
its towers stand in a straight row, all of equal height
questions.explanation: The chapter says the tall temple structure is made up of smaller copies of the full structure, on which there are even smaller copies, and so on — exactly the self-similarity of a fractal. Identical tiles or equal-height towers would not be self-similar.

questions.question: Where is the Kandariya Mahadev Temple, completed around 1025 CE?
options: Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu
Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh
Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh
Madurai, in Tamil Nadu
questions.explanation: The temple is in Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh. Madurai, Hampi, Rameswaram and Varanasi are listed separately as other places whose temples show fractal-like patterns.

questions.question: The chapter says fractal-like patterns also occur in temples in Madurai, Hampi, Rameswaram and Varanasi.
questions.explanation: After describing the Khajuraho temple, the chapter lists Madurai, Hampi, Rameswaram and Varanasi 'among many others' as places with fractal-like temple patterns.

questions.question: M.C. Escher's fractal print 'Smaller and Smaller' repeats which figure at ever smaller scales?
options: lizards
fishes
horses
eagles
questions.explanation: The chapter describes 'Smaller and Smaller' as exhibiting the identical pattern of lizards at smaller and smaller scales.

questions.question: M.C. Escher, called the modern maestro of fractal art, was a Polish artist whose prints also explored tiling.
questions.explanation: Escher was a Dutch artist (the Polish mathematician is Sierpinski). The rest of the statement is correct — his prints do explore tiling — which is what makes the wrong nationality easy to miss.

questions.question: Which statement about fractals is NOT correct?
options: fractals show the same or a similar pattern at smaller and smaller scales
a fractal looks completely different each time you zoom in closer
lightning and coastlines are natural examples of self-similarity
mathematical fractals are approached by repeating a geometric operation
questions.explanation: Zooming into a fractal shows the SAME pattern again, not something completely different — that is the whole point of self-similarity. The other three statements come straight from the chapter.

questions.question: To build the Sierpinski Carpet, a square is broken into how many smaller squares, and which part is removed?
options: 4 squares; the central square is removed
9 squares; the four corner squares are removed
9 squares; the central square is removed
8 squares; the central square is removed
questions.explanation: The square is broken into 9 smaller squares (3 × 3) and the central one is removed, leaving 8. Dividing into 4 is the Sierpinski Triangle's method; 8 is the number that remain, not the number of pieces.

questions.question: How many squares remain at Step 2 of the Sierpinski Carpet?
questions.explanation: R₂ = 8 × 8 = 64. 81 would be the count if nothing were removed (9²), 72 is 81 − 9, and 16 would come from the wrong multiplier 4.

questions.question: If Rₙ is the number of squares remaining at Step n of the Carpet, the correct recurrence is
options: Rₙ₊₁ = 8 × Rₙ
Rₙ₊₁ = 9 × Rₙ
Rₙ₊₁ = Rₙ + 8
Rₙ₊₁ = 8 × Rₙ − 1
questions.explanation: Every square that remains at Step n gives rise to 8 squares that remain at Step n + 1, so Rₙ₊₁ = 8Rₙ and Rₙ = 8ⁿ. Multiplying by 9 forgets the removed centre; adding 8 would grow far too slowly.

questions.question: How many holes does the Sierpinski Carpet have at Step 3?
questions.explanation: H₃ = 1 + 8 + 8² = 1 + 8 + 64 = 73. 64 is just the new holes made at Step 3; the old 9 holes from earlier steps remain too.

questions.question: Why does the hole count satisfy Hₙ₊₁ = Hₙ + Rₙ?
options: each existing hole splits into 8 smaller holes at the next step
each surviving square gains 8 new holes at the next step
each surviving square gains one new hole, and all old holes stay
old holes are filled in and new ones are made in their place
questions.explanation: Every square remaining at Step n has its centre removed at Step n + 1, giving Rₙ new holes, and every hole already present stays. So Hₙ₊₁ = Hₙ + Rₙ. Holes never split or get filled.

questions.question: A closed formula for the number of holes Hₙ in the Sierpinski Carpet is
questions.explanation: Hₙ = 1 + 8 + 8² + … + 8ⁿ⁻¹, and this sum equals (8ⁿ − 1)/7. Check: n = 2 gives 63/7 = 9 = 1 + 8, and n = 3 gives 511/7 = 73. The other formulas fail already at n = 1 or n = 2.

questions.question: Taking the starting square's area as 1 sq. unit, the area remaining at Step n of the Carpet is
questions.explanation: At each step every remaining square keeps 8 of its 9 ninths, so the area is multiplied by 8/9 each time: (8/9)ⁿ. At Step 1 this gives 8/9, matching one removed ninth.

questions.question: What is the total area of all the holes at Step 2 of the Carpet (starting area 1)?
questions.explanation: Remaining area at Step 2 is (8/9)² = 64/81, so the holes total 1 − 64/81 = 17/81. Equivalently: the big central hole is 1/9 = 9/81 and the 8 new small holes add 8/81. 9/81 alone is just the first hole.

questions.question: In the Sierpinski Carpet, 7 times the number of holes is always one less than the number of squares remaining.
questions.explanation: Hₙ = (8ⁿ − 1)/7 and Rₙ = 8ⁿ, so 7Hₙ = Rₙ − 1. Check Step 2: 7 × 9 = 63 = 64 − 1.

questions.question: The area of the Sierpinski Carpet shrinks by exactly one-ninth of the ORIGINAL square at every step.
questions.explanation: Each step removes one-ninth of the CURRENT remaining area, so the remaining area is multiplied by 8/9 each time. The amount removed gets smaller every step: 1/9, then 8/81, then 64/729.

questions.question: At which step does the area remaining in the Sierpinski Carpet first fall below half of the original?
options: Step 3
Step 4
Step 9
Step 6
questions.explanation: (8/9)⁵ ≈ 0.555 is still above one half, while (8/9)⁶ ≈ 0.493 is below it. So Step 6 is the first step with less than half the area remaining.

questions.question: How is an equilateral triangle divided into 4 identical equilateral triangles in the Sierpinski Gasket?
options: by joining the midpoints of its three sides
by joining each vertex to the centre of the triangle
by drawing the three altitudes of the triangle
by drawing one line parallel to each side at one-third height
questions.explanation: Joining the midpoints of the sides creates 4 identical equilateral triangles; the central one is then removed. Joining vertices to the centre gives 3 triangles, and altitudes give 6 right triangles.

questions.question: Why are the corner triangles made by joining the midpoints of an equilateral triangle themselves equilateral?
options: each is a right-angled triangle whose two legs are equal
each is isosceles (two half-sides) with a 60° angle between them
each has one side equal to a full side of the big triangle
each shares all three vertices with the central triangle
questions.explanation: A corner triangle has two sides that are halves of the big triangle's sides, so it is isosceles, and the angle between them is the 60° corner of the big triangle. An isosceles triangle with a 60° apex angle has all angles 60°, so it is equilateral.

questions.question: How many triangles remain at Step 3 of the Sierpinski Triangle?
questions.explanation: Each remaining triangle produces 3 at the next step, so the count is 3ⁿ: 1, 3, 9, 27. 64 would be the Carpet's count at Step 2.

questions.question: How many holes does the Sierpinski Triangle have at Step 3?
questions.explanation: Holes follow Hₙ₊₁ = Hₙ + Tₙ with T₀ = 1: H₁ = 1, H₂ = 1 + 3 = 4, H₃ = 4 + 9 = 13. 9 counts only the new holes at Step 3.

questions.question: A closed formula for the number of holes Hₙ in the Sierpinski Triangle is
questions.explanation: Hₙ = 1 + 3 + 3² + … + 3ⁿ⁻¹ = (3ⁿ − 1)/2. Check: n = 2 gives 8/2 = 4 and n = 3 gives 26/2 = 13, matching the step-by-step count.

questions.question: With the starting triangle's area as 1 sq. unit, the area remaining at Step n of the Sierpinski Triangle is
questions.explanation: Each step keeps 3 of the 4 equal pieces of every remaining triangle, so the area is multiplied by 3/4 per step: (3/4)ⁿ.

questions.question: After one step, which fractal has lost the larger fraction of its starting area?
options: the Sierpinski Carpet (loses 1/9) more than the Triangle (loses 1/4)
both lose the same fraction, one-eighth, of their starting area
the Triangle loses 1/3 and the Carpet loses 1/8 of the area
the Sierpinski Triangle (loses 1/4) more than the Carpet (loses 1/9)
questions.explanation: The Triangle removes 1 of 4 equal pieces (1/4 of the area); the Carpet removes 1 of 9 (1/9). Since 1/4 > 1/9, the Triangle loses more.

questions.question: Select ALL statements true for BOTH the Sierpinski Carpet and the Sierpinski Triangle.
options: holes made at one step remain in all later steps
the number of remaining pieces is multiplied by a fixed number each step
exactly one piece is removed in total at every step
the remaining area stays the same from step to step
questions.explanation: In both fractals old holes stay and the piece count is multiplied by 8 (Carpet) or 3 (Triangle) each step. One piece is removed from EACH remaining piece, not one in total, and the area shrinks every step.

questions.question: In the Sierpinski Triangle, each remaining triangle at Step n has side length 1/2ⁿ of the original side.
questions.explanation: Joining midpoints halves every side, so after n steps each small triangle's side is (1/2)ⁿ of the original.

questions.question: At the same step number, the Sierpinski Triangle always has MORE holes than the Sierpinski Carpet.
questions.explanation: Carpet holes: 1, 9, 73, …; Triangle holes: 1, 4, 13, …. They tie at Step 1 and afterwards the Carpet has more, because each of its pieces spawns 8 new pieces instead of 3.

questions.question: In one Koch step, each side is divided into 3 equal parts and then
options: an equilateral 'bump' replaces the middle part
a square bump is raised over the middle part
the middle part is cut out, leaving a gap
equilateral bumps replace all three parts
questions.explanation: An equilateral triangle is raised over the middle third and the middle third itself is removed — the side becomes a 'bump'-shaped line of 4 pieces. Nothing is left open, and only the middle part is changed.

questions.question: After one Koch step, each original side has been replaced by how many sides?
questions.explanation: The two outer thirds stay and the middle third becomes two sides of the raised triangle: 2 + 2 = 4 sides, each one-third of the original length.

questions.question: How many sides does the Koch shape have at Step 2 (starting from a triangle)?
questions.explanation: Sides multiply by 4 each step: 3 → 12 → 48. 27 and 36 come from multiplying by 3; 64 is 4³ and forgets the starting 3.

questions.question: A formula for the number of sides at Step n of the Koch Snowflake is
questions.explanation: Start with 3 sides and multiply by 4 at every step: 3 × 4ⁿ. Check n = 1: 12 sides, n = 2: 48 sides.

questions.question: With a starting side of 1 unit, the perimeter at Step 2 of the Koch Snowflake is
options: 4 units
16/3 units
48 units
64/9 units
questions.explanation: 48 sides each of length 1/9 give 48/9 = 16/3 units. Each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3: 3 → 4 → 16/3 → 64/9 (Step 3).

questions.question: A formula for the perimeter at Step n (starting side 1 unit) is
questions.explanation: Side count 3 × 4ⁿ times side length (1/3)ⁿ gives 3 × (4/3)ⁿ. (3/4)ⁿ would make the perimeter shrink; 3 × 4ⁿ ignores the shrinking side length.

questions.question: What happens to the perimeter of the Koch shape as the steps continue?
options: it settles down to a fixed value a little above 4
it stays equal to 3 at every single step
it shrinks because the pieces become smaller
it grows without bound, by a factor 4/3 each step
questions.explanation: Every step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3 > 1, so it keeps growing: 3, 4, 16/3, 64/9, … with no upper limit, even though the shape stays inside a bounded region.

questions.question: The Koch Snowflake was already encountered in Grade 6 Ganita Prakash.
questions.explanation: The chapter says: 'We have already encountered this fractal in Grade 6, Ganita Prakash.'

questions.question: At Step n of the Koch Snowflake, each side has length (1/4)ⁿ of the original side.
questions.explanation: Each side is divided into 3 equal parts, so lengths shrink by 1/3 per step: (1/3)ⁿ. The number 4 is how many sides each side becomes, not the shrink factor.

questions.question: Select ALL that are true of the Koch Snowflake step sequence.
options: each step multiplies the number of sides by 4
each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3
each step multiplies the side length by 1/4
each step multiplies the perimeter by 3
questions.explanation: Sides ×4 and side length ×1/3 together give perimeter ×4/3. Side length is divided by 3, not 4, and the perimeter is certainly not tripled.

questions.question: Whom does the chapter quote on building inventions entirely in the imagination before any real work?
options: Thomas Edison, American inventor
Nikola Tesla, Serbian-American engineer
M.C. Escher, Dutch graphic artist
Von Koch, Swedish mathematician
questions.explanation: The 'Build it in Your Imagination' section quotes Nikola Tesla (1856–1943), the Serbian-American engineer and inventor, who said he built and operated his devices entirely in his mind first.

questions.question: Cut off the four corners of a square, each cut joining the midpoints of two adjacent edges. What shape is left?
options: a regular octagon with eight equal sides
a rectangle twice as long as it is wide
a smaller square, turned through 45°
a rhombus whose angles are not right angles
questions.explanation: The four midpoints are the vertices of the leftover shape; its sides are the four cuts, all equal, meeting at right angles — a square tilted at 45°. Cutting only to the midpoints leaves 4 sides, not 8.

questions.question: In that corner-cutting of a square, how can the four cut-off corners be reassembled?
options: into an equilateral triangle with three equal sides
into a regular hexagon with six sides all equal
into a rectangle with two unequal pairs of sides
into another square, with the right angles at its centre
questions.explanation: Each corner is a right-angled isosceles triangle. Placing the four right angles together at one point makes 360°, and the four hypotenuses (the cut lines) form the boundary of a new square — the same size as the leftover square.

questions.question: Mark the sides of an equilateral triangle into thirds and cut off each corner as far as the marks. What shape results?
options: a six-sided regular hexagon
a smaller equilateral triangle
a four-sided square
a five-sided regular pentagon
questions.explanation: Each cut removes a small equilateral triangle of side one-third, leaving 6 sides all equal to one-third of the original side, with equal 120° angles: a regular hexagon.

questions.question: Mark a square's sides into thirds and cut off its corners as far as the marks. Which description is right?
options: a regular octagon with all eight sides equal
an octagon that is not regular — the slanted cut edges are longer
a regular hexagon with all six sides equal
an octagon that is not regular — the slanted cut edges are shorter
questions.explanation: Eight sides remain, so it is an octagon. Each cut is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 1/3 of a side, so it has length √2/3 ≈ 0.47 of a side — longer than the 1/3-side pieces left in the middle. Unequal sides means not regular.

questions.question: A solid has a rectangular profile from one viewpoint and a circular profile from another. Which solid fits?
options: a cone (party hat)
a cube (dice)
a sphere (ball)
a cylinder (can)
questions.explanation: A cylinder seen from the side is a rectangle and from the top is a circle. A cone gives a triangle and a circle, a cube gives squares/rectangles only, and a sphere always gives a circle.

questions.question: A solid has a circular profile from one viewpoint and a triangular profile from another. Which solid fits?
options: a cone (party hat)
a cylinder (can)
a square pyramid
a sphere (ball)
questions.explanation: A cone is a circle from directly above or below and a triangle from the side. A square pyramid gives a square and a triangle, and a cylinder gives a circle and a rectangle.

questions.question: A solid has a rectangular profile from one viewpoint and a triangular profile from another. Which solid fits?
options: a cone (party hat)
a triangular prism
a cylinder (can)
a square pyramid
questions.explanation: A triangular prism (like a tent) is a triangle from its end and a rectangle from the side. A cone's profiles are circle and triangle; a square pyramid's are square and triangle.

questions.question: A solid shows a trapezium-shaped profile from one viewpoint and a circular one from another. Which solid fits?
options: a cylinder standing upright
a square pyramid on its base
a bucket-shaped cut-off cone
a hemisphere (half a ball)
questions.explanation: A cone with its top sliced off parallel to the base (a bucket shape) is a circle from above and a trapezium from the side. A full cylinder gives a rectangle, and a hemisphere gives a semicircle, not a trapezium.

questions.question: For each pair of contrasting profiles in the chapter, exactly one solid can produce them.
questions.explanation: The chapter asks whether the solids are unique 'or can you come up with multiple possibilities?' — several solids can match. For example, both a sphere and a cylinder viewed from above give a circular profile.

questions.question: Which of these solids can NOT give a square profile from any viewpoint?
options: a sphere
a cube
a cylinder as tall as it is wide
a square pyramid
questions.explanation: A sphere's profile is a circle from every viewpoint. A cube shows a square face-on, a cylinder whose height equals its diameter is a square from the side, and a square pyramid is a square from above.

questions.question: Which description matches a VERTEX of a solid?
options: a flat surface forming the boundary
a point at which edges meet
a line segment forming the side of a face
a curved surface forming the boundary
questions.explanation: Faces are the flat surfaces of the boundary, edges are the line segments forming the sides of faces, and vertices are the points at which edges meet.

questions.question: In general, a prism has as its two opposite faces
options: two congruent polygons, with all other faces triangles
one polygon and one point, joined by triangular faces
two circles, joined by a single curved surface
two congruent polygons, with all other faces parallelograms
questions.explanation: A prism has two congruent polygons as opposite faces, with edges connecting corresponding vertices, so the other faces are parallelograms. Triangular side faces describe a pyramid; two circles describe a cylinder.

questions.question: Which name is also used for a triangular pyramid?
options: tetrahedron
octahedron
dodecahedron
triangular prism
questions.explanation: The chapter states that a triangular pyramid is also known as a tetrahedron (four faces). An octahedron has 8 faces and a dodecahedron 12.

questions.question: A prism whose congruent polygons have 10 sides has
options: 11 faces, 20 edges, 11 vertices
12 faces, 30 edges, 20 vertices
12 faces, 20 edges, 30 vertices
10 faces, 30 edges, 20 vertices
questions.explanation: Faces: 10 side faces + 2 ends = 12. Edges: 10 on each end polygon + 10 connecting edges = 30. Vertices: 10 + 10 = 20. The option 11/20/11 belongs to the 10-sided PYRAMID.

questions.question: A pyramid whose base has 10 sides has
options: 12 faces, 30 edges, 20 vertices
11 faces, 10 edges, 11 vertices
11 faces, 20 edges, 11 vertices
10 faces, 20 edges, 11 vertices
questions.explanation: Faces: 10 triangles + 1 base = 11. Edges: 10 base edges + 10 edges to the apex = 20. Vertices: 10 base vertices + 1 apex = 11. The 12/30/20 option is the 10-sided PRISM.

questions.question: For a prism built on n-sided polygons, the numbers of faces, edges and vertices are
questions.explanation: n side faces plus 2 ends give n + 2 faces; n + n polygon edges plus n connecting edges give 3n; two polygons give 2n vertices. Check with a cuboid (n = 4): 6, 12, 8.

questions.question: For a pyramid on an n-sided base, the numbers of faces, edges and vertices are
questions.explanation: n triangular faces + 1 base = n + 1 faces; n base edges + n edges to the apex = 2n; n base vertices + 1 apex = n + 1. Check with a square pyramid (n = 4): 5, 8, 5.

questions.question: Which solid has the same number of faces as vertices?
options: a pentagonal prism (7 and 10)
a triangular prism (5 and 6)
a pentagonal pyramid (6 and 6)
a cuboid, i.e. a box (6 and 8)
questions.explanation: Every pyramid has n + 1 faces and n + 1 vertices, so they always match: a pentagonal pyramid has 6 of each. Prisms have n + 2 faces but 2n vertices, which differ for n ≥ 3.

questions.question: An octahedron is made by joining two square pyramids at their square bases. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have?
options: 10 faces, 16 edges, 10 vertices
8 faces, 16 edges, 8 vertices
8 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices
8 faces, 12 edges, 6 vertices
questions.explanation: The two square bases disappear inside, leaving 4 + 4 = 8 triangular faces. Edges: the 4 shared base edges plus 4 + 4 slant edges = 12. Vertices: the 4 shared base corners plus 2 apexes = 6. Adding the two pyramids' counts (10/16/10) double-counts the shared base.

questions.question: A prism with hexagonal ends and a pyramid with a hexagonal base have the same number of edges.
questions.explanation: The hexagonal prism has 3 × 6 = 18 edges; the hexagonal pyramid has 2 × 6 = 12. (The pyramid has 7 faces and 7 vertices; the prism has 8 faces and 12 vertices.)

questions.question: Prisms and pyramids are named after the shape of their congruent polygons or base — for example triangular, pentagonal or hexagonal.
questions.explanation: The chapter says prisms are named by the shape of their congruent polygons (triangular, pentagonal, …) and pyramids by the shape of the base (triangular, square, pentagonal, …).

questions.question: Select ALL the solids that have exactly 5 faces.
options: a triangular prism
a square pyramid
a pentagonal pyramid
a cube
questions.explanation: Triangular prism: 3 + 2 = 5 faces. Square pyramid: 4 + 1 = 5 faces. A pentagonal pyramid has 6 faces and a cube has 6.

questions.question: What does the chapter call a net?
options: a flat shape that can be folded up to make the solid
a drawing of the solid as seen from the front
a wire frame that shows only the solid's edges
the shadow the solid casts on a flat wall
questions.explanation: A net is a shape on a flat surface that can be folded into the solid — equivalently, what you get by 'unfolding' a solid onto a plane.

questions.question: Which list names the solids the chapter says can be made from foldable flat materials such as paper, cardboard or metal sheet?
options: sphere, cuboid, cylinder, cone, prism, pyramid
cuboid, parallelopiped, cylinder, cone, prism, pyramid
cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone, prism, hemisphere
cube, sphere, parallelopiped, cone, prism, pyramid
questions.explanation: The chapter lists cuboid, parallelopiped, cylinder, cone, prism and pyramid. A sphere (or hemisphere) cannot be made from a flat sheet without wrinkles, gaps or overlaps.

questions.question: Why do packaging boxes carry extra flaps on some faces of their net?
options: the flaps are part of the net and count as extra faces
the flaps make the box heavier so it can stand upright
the flaps replace cello tape, which cannot stick to cardboard
the flaps stick to neighbouring faces when the sheet is flimsy
questions.explanation: For less sturdy materials like chart paper it helps to have extra flaps that can be stuck to adjacent faces; for cardboard, cello tape alone can join the faces. Flaps are not counted as part of the net.

questions.question: When we speak of the net of a solid, the extra flaps used to glue it together are counted as part of the net.
questions.explanation: The net is only the shape formed by unfolding the solid; supporting flaps used to actually build it are not part of the net.

questions.question: How many different nets does a cube have, counting rotations and flips of a net as the same?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that a cube has 11 possible net structures in total. 6 is the number of faces, and 12 the number of edges.

questions.question: Two nets of a cube are counted as the same net when
options: both contain exactly the same number of squares
one can be obtained from the other by a rotation or a flip
both fold into cubes of exactly the same size
both have four squares arranged in a straight row
questions.explanation: The chapter's rule: two nets are the same if one can be obtained from the other by rotating or flipping it. Every cube net has 6 squares and folds into the same-size cube, so those cannot be the test.

questions.question: A net of a cuboid with sides 5 cm, 3 cm and 1 cm is drawn. What is the total area of its six faces?
options: 23 cm²
15 cm²
54 cm²
46 cm²
questions.explanation: The faces come in pairs: 5 × 3 = 15, 5 × 1 = 5, 3 × 1 = 3, and 2 × (15 + 5 + 3) = 46 cm². 23 forgets to double, 15 is just one face, 54 is a cube of side 3.

questions.question: In the net of a cuboid with sides 6 cm, 3 cm and 2 cm, the rectangles are
options: 6×3, 6×2 and 3×2, two of each
6×3, 6×2 and 3×2, one of each
6×6, 3×3 and 2×2, two of each
6×3 and 3×2 only, three of each
questions.explanation: Opposite faces of a cuboid are equal, so the net has two 6 × 3, two 6 × 2 and two 3 × 2 rectangles — six faces in all with total area 2(18 + 12 + 6) = 72 cm².

questions.question: Which statement about cube nets is NOT correct?
options: there are several different nets that fold into a cube
any six squares joined edge to edge will fold into a cube
a cube net is made up of exactly six square faces
a net shows only the unfolded faces, not any gluing flaps
questions.explanation: Not every six-square arrangement works — a 2 × 3 block or a row of five, for instance, cannot fold into a cube — which is why the chapter asks you to test which figures are nets. Only 11 arrangements succeed.

questions.question: Select ALL the correct 'number of nets' facts from the chapter.
options: cube: 11 nets
regular tetrahedron: 2 nets
octahedron: 2 nets
dodecahedron: 11 nets
questions.explanation: The cube has 11 nets and the regular tetrahedron only 2. The octahedron also has 11 (not 2), and the dodecahedron has 43,380.

questions.question: A regular tetrahedron is a tetrahedron whose faces are all
options: isosceles triangles
right-angled triangles
equilateral triangles
congruent squares
questions.explanation: The chapter defines a regular tetrahedron as a tetrahedron whose faces are equilateral triangles. A solid with square faces is a cube.

questions.question: How many different nets does a regular tetrahedron have?
questions.explanation: The chapter states a regular tetrahedron has only 2 possible nets (a row of four triangles, and a triangle with three triangles around it). 4 is its number of faces; 11 belongs to the cube.

questions.question: A dodecahedron is a solid all of whose faces are
options: hexagons
pentagons
triangles
squares
questions.explanation: The chapter asks whether a solid can have all pentagonal faces and answers yes — the dodecahedron. Triangles give the tetrahedron/octahedron, squares the cube.

questions.question: How many nets does a dodecahedron have, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Mathematicians have determined exactly how many nets a dodecahedron has: 43,380. The number 11 is the count for a cube or octahedron.

questions.question: Unroll a cylinder after cutting it along its height. Its net consists of
options: one circle and a sector
two circles and a triangle
one circle and a rectangle
two circles and a rectangle
questions.explanation: The two circular faces unfold as circles and the curved surface, cut along the height, opens into a rectangle. A circle plus a sector is the net of a cone.

questions.question: In the net of a cylinder, the two side lengths of the rectangle are
options: the height of the cylinder and the circumference of its circular face
the height of the cylinder and the diameter of its circular face
the height of the cylinder and the radius of its circular face
twice the height of the cylinder and the circumference of its face
questions.explanation: One side is the cut along the height; the other wraps once around the circle, so it equals the circle's circumference (not its diameter or radius).

questions.question: When a cone is slit open along a slant line l from its apex O and unrolled, its curved surface becomes
options: a rectangle with one side equal to l
a portion of a circle with centre O
a triangle with its apex at O
a complete circle with centre O
questions.explanation: After unrolling, the boundary of the net is a portion of a circle (a sector) centred at the apex O, with radius equal to the slant length l.

questions.question: Why is the boundary of the unrolled cone an arc of a circle centred at O?
options: the slit line l has the same length as the base radius
the apex O sits exactly above the centre of the base
all points of the base boundary are equally far from O
the base of a cone is a circle, so its net must be one too
questions.explanation: The chapter's reasoning: every point on the boundary of the base circle is at the same distance (the slant length) from O, so after unrolling those points all lie on a circle centred at O.

questions.question: A paper cutout can be made that wraps perfectly around a ball without wrinkles, gaps or overlaps.
questions.explanation: The chapter invites you to try and discover that it cannot be done — a sphere has no net, unlike cubes, cones and cylinders.

questions.question: Select ALL the solids the chapter's summary says can be obtained by folding suitable nets.
options: octahedron
cone
sphere
ball-shaped globe
questions.explanation: The summary lists cuboids, tetrahedrons, cylinders, cones, prisms, pyramids and octahedrons. A sphere (a globe is a sphere) has no net — no paper cutout wraps it without wrinkles or gaps.

questions.question: On a plane, the shortest path between two points is
options: any path that follows the grid lines
the straight line segment joining them
the arc of a circle through both points
the path that runs along the boundary
questions.explanation: The chapter starts from this known fact and then asks what the shortest path is on the SURFACE of a cuboid.

questions.question: What is the key idea for finding the shortest surface path from the ant to the laddu?
options: cut straight through the inside of the cuboid
walk only along the edges of the cuboid
draw a straight line on a net of the cuboid
measure the longest diagonal of the cuboid
questions.explanation: A path on the surface corresponds to a path of the same length on the net, so the shortest surface path is the one that becomes a straight line on a suitable net. The ant may travel only along the surface, not through the inside.

questions.question: A path marked on the cuboid does NOT become a straight line on the net. What can we conclude?
options: it is not the shortest path between those points
it is the shortest path, since it stays on the surface
it is exactly as long as the straight-line path
nothing — the net tells us nothing about length
questions.explanation: On the net the shortest path is the straight line. A surface path whose image is not straight is longer than that line, so it cannot be the shortest. This is the chapter's second ant–laddu case.

questions.question: On one unfolding, the straight segment from ant to laddu runs OUTSIDE the net. What does this mean?
options: the ant cannot reach the laddu along the surface
it matches no surface path; unfold another way
that unfolding has found the shortest path
the segment is still a valid path on the cuboid
questions.explanation: A line that leaves the net does not correspond to any path on the cuboid, so that unfolding is useless here. Unfolding the cuboid differently gives a straight segment inside the net — 'the way a cuboid is unfolded matters'.

questions.question: In the 30 cm × 12 cm × 12 cm box problem, one unfolding gives d² = 24² + 32². The distance d is
options: 56 cm
48 cm
40 cm
42 cm
questions.explanation: 24² = 576 and 32² = 1024, so d² = 1600 and d = 40 cm. 56 is 24 + 32 (adding instead of using the theorem); 42 is the length of a different unfolding.

questions.question: For the same box, one unfolding gives a straight ant–laddu line of 42 cm and another gives 40 cm. The shortest surface path is
options: 40 cm, found by comparing all unfoldings
42 cm, because it goes straight over the top
41 cm, the average of the two unfoldings
82 cm, adding the two unfoldings together
questions.explanation: Different unfoldings give different straight-line lengths, so we must list them all and take the smallest — here 40 cm beats 42 cm, even though the 42 cm path 'looks' direct.

questions.question: The way a cuboid is unfolded has no effect on the straight-line distance between the two points on the net.
questions.explanation: The chapter shows unfoldings of the same box giving 42 cm, 40 cm and other lengths — 'the lengths of the line segments between the ant and the laddu are different'. The unfolding matters.

questions.question: To be sure of the shortest surface path, one should list the different possible unfoldings and compare their straight-line lengths.
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes: 'we have to carefully list all the possible different unfoldings to find the answer!'

questions.question: Which statement about shortest paths on a cuboid is NOT correct?
options: every path on the net corresponds to an equal-length path on the cuboid
the straight line through the inside of the cuboid is an allowed path
different unfoldings can give different straight-line lengths
a path that is straight on a suitable net is a shortest surface path
questions.explanation: The ant lives on the surface and may travel only along it, so a tunnel through the interior is not allowed. The other three statements are exactly the chapter's reasoning.

questions.question: Select ALL that are true about using a net to find the ant's shortest path.
options: a surface path and its net image have equal length
the shortest surface path is straight on some net
every unfolding gives the same straight-line length
a straight line that leaves the net is still a valid path
questions.explanation: Lengths are preserved by unfolding and the shortest path appears straight on a suitable net. But unfoldings differ in length (42 vs 40 cm), and a segment leaving the net corresponds to no path.

questions.question: Point O on plane M is called the projection of point P when
options: the line OP is parallel to the plane M
O is the centre point of the plane M
the line OP is perpendicular to the plane M
OP is the longest line from P to the plane
questions.explanation: A line from P meets the plane at O; if OP is perpendicular to the plane, O is the projection of P. Perpendicular gives the shortest, not longest, line from P to M.

questions.question: 'OP is perpendicular to the plane M' means, by the chapter's definition, that
options: for ONE particular line OX in the plane, angle POX = 90°
angle POX = 90° only for lines OX outside the plane
OP has the same length as every line OX in the plane
for ANY line OX drawn in the plane, angle POX = 90°
questions.explanation: Perpendicularity to a plane requires a right angle with EVERY line OX in the plane through O, not just one.

questions.question: A line of length l has a projection of length p (Fig. 4.3, with AE ⊥ BC and AECD a rectangle). Which is correct?
options: p ≥ l: projecting onto a plane spreads the line out
p ≤ l: AE is a leg and AB the hypotenuse of triangle AEB
p = l always: projecting onto a plane keeps length
p = l/2: E must be the midpoint of segment BC
questions.explanation: AE = DC = p because AECD is a rectangle, and ∠AEB = 90°, so in right triangle AEB the hypotenuse AB = l is at least as long as the leg AE = p. A projection is never longer than the line.

questions.question: When is the projection of a line exactly as long as the line itself?
options: when the line is perpendicular to the plane
when the line passes through the plane
when the line is parallel to the plane
when the line is tilted at 45° to the plane
questions.explanation: If the line is parallel to the plane, points A and B are equally far from it and p = l. A perpendicular line projects to a single point (p = 0), and a 45° tilt shortens it.

questions.question: Which of these can NEVER be the projection of a parallelogram?
options: a quadrilateral that is not a parallelogram
a parallelogram of a quite different shape
a rectangle whose sides differ in length
a line segment, if the shape is seen edge-on
questions.explanation: Parallel lines project to parallel lines, so a parallelogram's projection always has two pairs of parallel sides — a parallelogram (possibly a rectangle), or a segment if its plane is perpendicular to the projection plane. A trapezium or kite is impossible.

questions.question: The projection of a pair of parallel lines is
options: parallel only when the lines are parallel to the plane
always a pair of parallel lines
a pair of lines meeting at one point
always a pair of perpendicular lines
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the projection of a pair of parallel lines always remains parallel, whatever the orientation — a fact later used for isometric drawing.

questions.question: Select ALL shapes that can be the projection of a square, depending on its orientation.
options: a rectangle
a line segment
a triangle
a pentagon
questions.explanation: Tilting a square about one side shortens the other pair of sides, giving a rectangle; turning it edge-on to the plane gives a segment. Parallel sides stay parallel, so the projection is always a parallelogram (or a segment) — it can never become a triangle or a pentagon.

questions.question: What can be said about the projection of an n-sided regular polygon?
options: always another regular n-sided polygon
a polygon with 2n sides, twice as many
an n-gon, not necessarily regular
a circle, whenever n is large enough
questions.explanation: The projection is made of the projections of the n sides, so it is a polygon with (at most) n sides, but different sides are shortened by different amounts, so it is generally not regular.

questions.question: If an object passes perpendicularly through a plane and makes a hole, the hole has the same shape as the object's projection on that plane.
questions.explanation: The chapter states exactly this: the shape of the hole would be the same as the shape of the projection of the object — like the cartoon character's outline in the wall.

questions.question: Two different objects can produce exactly the same projection on a plane.
questions.explanation: Fig. 4.6 shows different lines and different cuboids giving identical projections: 'a given projection is not made by a unique object'. That is why three views are usually taken.

questions.question: Which object gives the same projection as a cone viewed from directly above (a circle)?
options: a cube with side equal to the radius
a square pyramid of the same height
a triangular prism of the same height
a cylinder with the same base radius
questions.explanation: From above, a cylinder projects to a circle of its base radius — identical to the cone's. A cube and square pyramid give squares and a triangular prism gives a rectangle or triangle.

questions.question: The front view of an object is its projection on which plane?
options: the vertical plane in front of the object
the horizontal plane below the object
the side plane beside the object
a slanted plane above the object
questions.explanation: The vertical plane in front of the object gives the front view; the horizontal plane below gives the top view; the side plane gives the side view.

questions.question: The top view is the projection on
options: the vertical plane in front of the object
the horizontal plane below the object
the side plane beside the object
a plane placed above the object
questions.explanation: The top view is the projection on the horizontal plane, which the chapter places BELOW the object — it shows what the object looks like from above.

questions.question: Why does the chapter take three mutually perpendicular projections of an object?
options: one projection is always enough; the others are decoration
three projections together give the object's volume directly
a single projection does not identify the object uniquely
the three projections of any object are always identical
questions.explanation: Since different objects can share one projection, taking front, top and side views together pins the object down much better.

questions.question: A line segment stands vertically (along the height direction). Its three views are
options: full length in the front and side views; a point in the top view
full length in the top view; a point in the front and side views
full length in all three views
a point in all three views
questions.explanation: A vertical segment is parallel to the vertical and side planes, so those views show its full length; it is perpendicular to the horizontal plane, so the top view is a point.

questions.question: A line segment runs left-to-right along the length direction. Its three views are
options: full length in the front and side views; a point in the top view
full length in the front and top views; a point in the side view
full length in the top and side views; a point in the front view
full length only in the front view; points in the other two
questions.explanation: The length direction is parallel to both the vertical (front) and horizontal (top) planes, so both show the full length, while the side plane is perpendicular to it, giving a point.

questions.question: A cylinder stands on its circular base. Its front view and top view are
options: front: a circle; top: a rectangle
front: a rectangle; top: a rectangle
front: a rectangle; top: a circle
front: a triangle; top: a circle
questions.explanation: Seen from the front, a standing cylinder is a rectangle (height × diameter); from above it is a circle.

questions.question: A square pyramid stands on its base. Its front view and top view are
options: front: a triangle; top: a square
front: a square; top: a triangle
front: a triangle; top: a triangle
front: a rectangle; top: a square
questions.explanation: From the front a square pyramid is a triangle; from above you see its square base (with the slant edges meeting at the centre).

questions.question: The front, top and side views formalise the idea of a solid's profile from different viewpoints.
questions.explanation: The chapter says these projections 'formalise the notion of profiles that we explored in an earlier section'.

questions.question: The side view of an object is its projection on the horizontal plane.
questions.explanation: The side view is the projection on the SIDE plane; the horizontal plane gives the top view.

questions.question: Which of these solids, standing on a base, have a circular top view? Select ALL.
options: a cylinder
a cone
a cube
a square pyramid
questions.explanation: Both a cylinder and a cone have a circular base, so from above each projects to a circle. A cube and a square pyramid project to squares.

questions.question: A cube is seen with one face parallel to the vertical plane and its edges parallel to the three planes. Its three views are
options: a square, a rectangle and a hexagon
a square and two rectangles
three identical squares
a hexagon, a square and a triangle
questions.explanation: With the cube aligned to the planes, each view is a face-on look at a square face, so all three views are equal squares. A hexagon appears only in the tilted isometric orientation.

questions.question: Shine a torch at an object, perpendicular to a wall. The shadow on the wall is
options: exactly the same as the projection, always
completely unrelated to the projection shape
always smaller than the projection shape
like the projection, but maybe scaled or stretched
questions.explanation: The chapter says the shadow is quite similar to the projection but may be scaled up, stretched or slightly distorted depending on how the object is held.

questions.question: As the torch is moved farther from the object (still pointing perpendicular to the wall), the shadow
options: becomes more and more like the projection
grows larger and larger without any limit
disappears completely from the wall
turns into a perfect circle
questions.explanation: With an imaginary extremely powerful torch moved far away, the shadow becomes indistinguishable from the projection of the object onto the wall plane.

questions.question: Why does the shadow's size change when a nearby torch is moved closer or farther?
options: the wall absorbs more light when the torch is far away, shrinking the shadow
a near torch's rays fan out, so a close object blocks a wider cone of light
the object physically expands slightly in the warmth of the torch light
the shadow always copies the size of the torch's round glass front
questions.explanation: Rays from a nearby torch fan out from a point. The closer the object is to that point, the wider the bundle of rays it blocks, so the shadow is larger; farther away the rays are nearly parallel and the shadow approaches the projection.

questions.question: Why does the chapter call the Sun 'an extremely powerful and distant torch'?
options: it is so bright that its shadows have no edges at all
it moves across the sky, so shadows rotate during the day
it is so far away that its rays reach us practically parallel
it is so large that it lights every side of an object at once
questions.explanation: A very distant light source sends almost parallel rays, which is exactly the situation in which a shadow becomes indistinguishable from a projection.

questions.question: When sunlight falls perpendicular to a plane, the shadows it casts on that plane are indistinguishable from projections.
questions.explanation: The chapter states this directly and uses it to let you 'see' projections with a cutout in sunlight.

questions.question: Hold a parallelogram cutout in sunlight in any orientation. Its shadow is
options: sometimes a trapezium
sometimes a kite shape
always a rectangle
always a parallelogram
questions.explanation: No matter how you orient the parallelogram, its shadow remains a parallelogram, because the projection of parallel lines stays parallel. It need not be a rectangle.

questions.question: Which statement about shadows is NOT correct?
options: a shadow may be scaled up compared with the projection
a shadow always has exactly the same size as the object
a shadow may be slightly distorted depending on how the object is held
a shadow under perpendicular sunlight matches the projection
questions.explanation: A torch shadow can be enlarged, stretched or distorted, so it does not always equal the object's size. The other three statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: Select ALL the ways a torch shadow may differ from the exact projection, according to the chapter.
options: it may be scaled up
it may be stretched
a straight edge may become a curve
a parallelogram may become a trapezium
questions.explanation: The chapter says the shadow may be scaled up, stretched or slightly distorted. Straight edges stay straight and parallel edges stay parallel, so a parallelogram never becomes a trapezium.

questions.question: What does 'isometric' mean in Greek?
options: equal angles
same shape
equal measure
three directions
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that 'isometric' means 'equal measure' in Greek — the projections of all the cube's edges have equal length.

questions.question: An isometric projection of a cube is an orientation in which
options: only one face of the cube can be seen
all of its faces project as squares
the cube is seen exactly face-on
all its edges project to equal lengths
questions.explanation: In the isometric projection the lengths of the projections of ALL the edges are equal. Seen face-on, only edges in one direction keep their length.

questions.question: How can you physically produce the isometric projection of a cube?
options: balance it on a corner vertex and project it onto the floor
lay it flat on a face and project it down to the floor
balance it on one edge and project it onto a wall
hold one face parallel to the wall and project it there
questions.explanation: Imagine balancing a cube perfectly on one of its corner vertices and projecting it down to the floor plane — that projection is isometric.

questions.question: The isometric representation of a cube is a
options: square
regular hexagon
rectangle
regular octagon
questions.explanation: Balanced on a corner, a cube projects to a regular hexagon; this hexagon is the basis of the isometric grid.

questions.question: If the cube were made of glass, in its isometric projection
options: only 9 edges would be visible
only the 6 outline edges would be visible
all 12 edges would be visible
only 3 edges would be visible
questions.explanation: A glass cube hides nothing, so all 12 edges appear: 6 form the hexagon's outline and the other 6 are 'spokes' from the hexagon's vertices to its centre (3 from the top vertex, 3 from the bottom vertex, which project to the same central point).

questions.question: Isometric grids let engineers measure lengths along which three primary directions?
options: length, depth and height
length, width and diagonal
height, slant and diagonal
radius, diameter and circumference
questions.explanation: Fig. 4.7 labels the three primary directions as length, depth and height; isometric grids make it easy to measure along all three.

questions.question: On the isometric grid the edges appear in three orientations. The height axis is drawn as
options: the slanting / direction
the vertical | direction
the slanting \ direction
the horizontal — direction
questions.explanation: Height is associated with the vertical grid direction |, while depth and length take the two slanting directions. There is no horizontal line on an isometric grid.

questions.question: Why is the correspondence between isometric-paper directions and the solid's axes so effective?
options: every angle of the solid is kept exactly the same size in the drawing
hidden edges are removed automatically, so nothing needs erasing
parallel edges stay parallel and unit lengths along all axes project equal
every face is drawn with its true area and its true shape
questions.explanation: Parallel lines project to parallel lines, so the three families of parallel edges become the three grid directions, and the isometric nature makes unit distances along the three axes project to equal lengths. Angles and areas are NOT preserved.

questions.question: How many basic shapes does Tetris have, and what are they?
options: 4, the ways of arranging four squares
5, the ways of arranging five squares
7, the ways of arranging three squares
5, the ways of arranging four squares
questions.explanation: Fig. 4.8 shows the five basic Tetris shapes, corresponding to the different ways of arranging four squares.

questions.question: Every way of gluing four identical cubes together face to face is one of the five flat Tetris shapes.
questions.explanation: The chapter asks whether there are additional ways beyond the five flat ones — and there are: cubes can be glued so the shape does not lie flat (for example three in an L with the fourth on top of the corner).

questions.question: Why does the 'impossible triangle' drawn on an isometric grid fool the eye?
options: one drawing fits many solids, so parts can join impossibly
it is a genuine solid that can really be built from cubes
isometric drawings cannot show any depth at all
the grid lines of the paper are drawn at a wrong angle
questions.explanation: A projection does not determine a unique object. Each corner of the triangle is a perfectly realisable piece, but the pieces are joined in a way no single solid can achieve — the drawing exploits the information lost in projecting.

questions.question: Select ALL that are true about drawing on isometric paper.
options: moving vertically on the paper corresponds to the height axis of the solid
lengths along the three primary axes can be read off the grid
the isometric view of a cube is a square
isometric grids are rarely used in engineering
questions.explanation: Vertical on the paper = height axis, and the grid lets you measure along length, depth and height. The isometric view of a cube is a regular hexagon, and isometric grids are widely used in engineering.

questions.question: Which shapes can the projection of a cube make under different orientations? Select ALL.
options: a square
a hexagon
a triangle
a pentagon
questions.explanation: Face-on a cube projects to a square (or a rectangle when turned about one edge-direction); balanced on a corner it projects to a hexagon. Its outline never has 3 or 5 sides.
